_doc: English source strings for localized pages. Placeholders in {braces} must be kept exactly. Food tokens: {q} = the food as a sentence/question subject (e.g. 'cooked rice'; in ES/PT/FR with article: 'el arroz cocido'); {Q} = same with a capital first letter; {o} = the food as a grammatical object (German accusative, otherwise same as q); {n} = bare display name. Values that are [singular, plural] pairs are chosen by the food's grammatical number. Temperatures on localized pages are Celsius first.

freeze.dYes: Quality holds for about {d} at −18 °C (0 °F). Frozen food stays safe indefinitely; only quality declines.
freeze.dCooking: Quality holds for about {d} at −18 °C (0 °F). Texture changes, so use it in cooked dishes.
freeze.dNo: Freezing is not recommended for this food; texture breaks down or the result is not reliable.
freeze.dNoFigure: FoodKeeper gives no freezer time for this food.
freeze.afterThaw: After thawing in the fridge, use within {d}.

leftOut.tDiscard: Perishable food left at room temperature for more than 2 hours (1 hour above 32 °C / 90 °F) should be thrown away. Bacteria multiply fastest between 4 °C and 60 °C, and reheating does not remove every toxin they make.
leftOut.tKeep: This food is shelf-stable. A night on the counter is fine — keep it cool, dry and out of the sun.
leftOut.tShort: It keeps {p} at room temperature, so one night out is usually fine. It is not shelf-stable, though: use it soon or move it somewhere cooler.
leftOut.tHours: It keeps only {p} at room temperature. Left out longer, or overnight, it should be thrown away.
leftOut.tRipe: It can ripen on the counter. Once cut or cooked, the 2-hour rule applies.
leftOut.tOpened: Once opened, it belongs in the fridge. A night at room temperature speeds spoilage; if it smells, looks or tastes off, throw it out.
leftOut.tCaution: Not a high-risk food, but a night out shortens its fridge life. Refrigerate it and use it soon.

method.title: How We Verify Our Numbers | Gunther Heller
method.desc: Where our storage times come from (USDA FoodKeeper), how we turn them into answers and how to report a wrong number.
method.p1: Every storage time on this site comes from FoodKeeper, the storage database published by the US Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS). It is a public-domain government dataset.
method.p2: We import every FoodKeeper product and keep its pantry, fridge and freezer times, including the separate times after opening. We never invent a duration: if FoodKeeper has no figure, the page says so.
method.p3: Where FoodKeeper gives no room-temperature time for perishable food, we apply the FSIS rule: discard it after 2 hours at room temperature, or 1 hour above 32 °C (90 °F). Freezer times are about quality; food kept at −18 °C (0 °F) stays safe indefinitely.
method.p4: Translations are reviewed for accuracy; the numbers are identical in every language. To report an error, email {email}.

meat: A sour, sulphur or ammonia smell, even faint.
Sticky or slimy surface that stays after rinsing.
Grey-green or brown patches spreading across the meat.
A bloated or leaking pack, or past the date by more than the fridge window.
seafood: Strong fishy, sour or ammonia odour. Fresh seafood smells of the sea.
Mushy flesh that does not spring back, or a milky slime.
Dull, grey or yellowing flesh; dark edges.
Live shellfish with open shells that do not close when tapped.
cooked: Sour, yeasty or 'off' instead of how it smelled when cooked.
Slimy film, or liquid separating where it should not.
Dull or darkened patches, or any discoloured spots.
Any fuzzy growth — discard the whole container, not just the spot.
cured: Sour or rancid smell instead of smoky or salty.
Slick, slimy surface on slices or links.
Grey, green or iridescent patches that spread.
Fuzzy spots on sliced or cooked products — discard.
dairy: Sour or cheesy smell when it should be clean and mild.
Lumps, curdling or a thick, slimy body.
Yellowing or a pink, green or grey tinge.
Sour or bitter at the first sip — stop and discard.
cheese: Ammonia or a sharp sour smell beyond the cheese's usual aroma.
Slimy surface, or very dry and cracked all the way through.
Darkened or yellowed edges, or new colours that are not part of the cheese.
On hard cheese, cut 1 inch around the spot. On soft or shredded cheese, discard.
eggs: A sulphur smell when cracked — unmistakable, discard.
Pink, green or iridescent whites or yolks.
Shows age only. A floating egg is old; check the smell before deciding.
produce: Soft, mushy or leaking spots, or wrinkled skin with soft flesh.
Dark bruising that spreads, or browning inside.
White, grey or green fuzz — discard soft produce; cut firm produce generously.
leafy: A sour or rotting smell from the bag or bunch.
Slimy, wet or wilted leaves that do not perk up in cold water.
Any fuzzy growth — discard the bag.
bakery: Hard and dry is stale but safe; damp or sticky is not.
Discoloured spots on the crust or crumb.
Any visible mould — discard the whole item; roots spread unseen.
dry: Clumping from moisture, or a damp feel.
Webbing, holes, or tiny insects in the bag.
Flat, stale or bitter taste — quality is gone even if it is safe.
fat: Rancid: like crayons, paint or old nuts.
Sticky or gummy residue around the lid.
Darkened or cloudy where it should be clear.
condiment: Fermented, yeasty or sour beyond the product's usual tang.
Separation that does not stir back, or a slimy layer.
Darkening or a change in colour at the top of the jar.
Any fuzz on the surface or lid — discard the jar.
drink: Vinegary, sour or musty instead of fresh.
Flat, sour or bitter — quality is gone.
Cloudiness, sediment or film that was not there before.
Bulging carton, cap or can — discard.
frozen: Dry, greyish-white patches. Safe, but trim them off.
Heavy ice inside the pack means it has thawed and refrozen.
Torn packaging lets air in and speeds quality loss.
baby: Sour or off smell in prepared formula or food.
Separation that does not mix back, or clumps.
Jar lids that do not pop on opening, or damaged pouches — discard.

meat: Freeze on or before the last fridge day; the earlier, the better the texture.
Overwrap the store pack in foil or a freezer bag, or vacuum-seal; squeeze out air.
Thaw in the fridge (about 24 hours per 5 lb), or in cold water and cook right away.
seafood: Freeze as fresh as possible, ideally the day you buy it.
Wrap tightly in plastic, then a freezer bag; press out the air and date it.
Thaw overnight in the fridge or sealed in cold water; never on the counter.
cooked: Cool quickly: shallow containers, into the fridge or freezer within 2 hours.
Portion into freezer bags or airtight tubs, leave headspace for liquids, and label with the date.
Thaw in the fridge and reheat to 165°F (74°C) until steaming.
cured: Freeze in the original vacuum pack if unopened; otherwise wrap slices in plastic and foil.
Freeze in meal-size portions so you only thaw what you need.
Thaw in the fridge; texture of sliced meats softens slightly after freezing.
dairy: Pour off a little to leave room for expansion, then seal tightly.
Freeze flat or upright and date it.
Thaw in the fridge and shake or whisk well; use for cooking or baking.
cheese: Cut or portion into blocks of ½ lb or less, or freeze shredded cheese in its bag.
Wrap in plastic, then a freezer bag, pressing out air.
Thaw in the fridge; it will be crumblier, so use it melted or cooked.
eggs: Never freeze eggs in the shell.
Beat whole eggs (or separate whites and yolks) and pour into a lidded container or ice-cube tray.
Thaw in the fridge and use only in dishes cooked to 160°F (71°C).
produce: Wash, dry and cut into pieces; blanch most vegetables for 1–3 minutes first.
Spread on a tray to freeze individually, then bag and press out air.
Use from frozen in cooking or smoothies; thawed produce is soft.
leafy: Leafy greens and herbs lose their crunch when frozen.
For cooking, blanch greens or chop herbs into ice-cube trays with oil or water.
Add straight from frozen to soups, sauces and stir-fries.
bakery: Freeze on the day you buy or bake it, once fully cool.
Wrap tightly in plastic, then a freezer bag; slice bread first so you can take what you need.
Thaw at room temperature in the wrap, or toast or warm from frozen.
dry: Freezing is optional for dry goods; it mainly stops pests and rancidity.
Use an airtight container or a well-sealed freezer bag.
Let it come to room temperature before opening to avoid condensation.
fat: Freeze in an airtight container or the original sealed pack.
Portion first (cubes or small jars) so you thaw only what you need.
Thaw in the fridge; fats and nuts can be used straight from frozen.
condiment: Most condiments keep well in the fridge and do not need freezing.
If freezing, use ice-cube trays or small containers and label them.
Thaw in the fridge and stir well; emulsions may separate.
drink: Leave headspace in a freezer-safe container; liquids expand.
Freeze in ice-cube trays for small portions.
Thaw in the fridge and shake well before using.
frozen: Keep it at 0°F (-18°C) or colder in the original pack.
Reseal opened bags tightly or move to a freezer bag.
Cook from frozen as the package directs, or thaw in the fridge.
baby: Freeze only what the guidance allows, in clean, sealed containers.
Label with the date and time.
Thaw in the fridge or in warm water; never microwave, and do not refreeze.

meat: Refrigerate at 40°F (4°C) or below as soon as you get home; bottom shelf, so juices cannot drip.
Keep it in the store pack until you use it, or overwrap for the freezer.
Cook or freeze within the fridge window; the clock starts at purchase.
seafood: Keep on ice or in the coldest part of the fridge, at 40°F (4°C) or below.
Store live shellfish in a bowl covered with a damp cloth, never in water or sealed plastic.
Cook or freeze within the fridge window.
cooked: Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F) in shallow, airtight containers.
Keep the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C); the door shelf is the warmest spot.
Reheat leftovers to 165°F (74°C) and only reheat what you will eat.
cured: Keep refrigerated at 40°F (4°C) or below, even though it is cured.
Once opened, rewrap tightly or move to an airtight container.
Use within the opened window regardless of the package date.
dairy: Store on an inside shelf, not the door, at 40°F (4°C) or below.
Close the container tightly; dairy absorbs fridge odours.
Pour what you need and return it to the fridge right away.
cheese: Wrap in wax or parchment paper, then loosely in plastic, so it can breathe.
Store in the cheese drawer or a lower shelf at 40°F (4°C) or below.
Use a clean knife each time to avoid introducing mould.
eggs: Keep eggs in their carton on an inside shelf, not the door.
Store at 40°F (4°C) or below; do not wash them before storing.
Refrigerate hard-boiled eggs within 2 hours of cooking.
produce: Store unwashed; wash just before eating.
Keep ethylene producers (apples, bananas, avocados) away from produce that over-ripens.
Refrigerate once cut, in a covered container.
leafy: Store dry, wrapped in a paper towel inside a bag or container.
Keep in the crisper drawer at 40°F (4°C) or below.
Stand herbs like cilantro and parsley in a glass of water in the fridge, loosely covered.
bakery: Keep at room temperature in a bread box or sealed bag for the best texture.
Refrigeration slows mould but makes bread stale faster.
Freeze what you will not eat in time.
dry: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dark, dry place.
Keep away from the stove and dishwasher, where heat and humidity speed spoilage.
Write the opening date on the pack.
fat: Keep in a cool, dark place, tightly closed, away from heat.
Refrigerating nuts, seeds and nut oils extends shelf life significantly.
Smell before using; rancidity is a quality problem you can detect.
condiment: Refrigerate after opening unless the label says otherwise.
Use a clean utensil each time; crumbs and double-dipping shorten shelf life.
Wipe the rim and close the lid tightly.
drink: Store unopened in a cool, dark place.
Refrigerate after opening and close tightly.
Keep away from light and heat, which flatten flavour.
frozen: Keep your freezer at 0°F (-18°C) or colder.
Do not let it thaw and refreeze on the way home; shop for frozen food last.
Reseal opened bags to prevent freezer burn.
baby: Follow the label and your pediatrician's instructions first.
Refrigerate prepared or opened products right away.
Discard anything left in a bottle or bowl the baby has fed from.

viz.glanceNote: Bars show the longest recommended time for each place. Scale runs from 1 hour to 2 years.
viz.levelNote: Based on the longest fridge or pantry time.

viz.edgeText: It's inside the safe window but near the end. Eat it today or freeze it now.
viz.tossText: Past the recommended fridge time. Even if it looks and smells fine, throw it out.
